task: Use the Cambridge Dictionary to understand the rules for forming and using comparative and superlative adjectives in English Grammar, including example sentences.
answer: Used the Cambridge Dictionary British Grammar article 'Comparison: adjectives (bigger, biggest, more interesting)' (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/comparison-adjectives-bigger-biggest-more-interesting, under Grammar > Adjectives and adverbs > Adjectives > Comparative and superlative adjectives). Rules learned: (1) Comparative adjectives compare one person/thing with another and are normally followed by 'than'; superlative adjectives compare one person/thing with the whole group. (2) One-syllable adjectives form comparatives/superlatives with -er/-est (tall-taller-tallest, old-older-oldest), with spelling rules such as consonant doubling (big-bigger-biggest) and -e endings (nice-nicer-nicest). (3) Two-syllable adjectives may take -er/-est or more/most; longer adjectives use more/most (more interesting, the most frightening), and less/least express lower degree. (4) Irregular forms include good-better-best and bad-worse-worst. (5) Usage: much/a lot/far + comparative; 'the -er, the -er' and 'the more, the more' constructions; 'the' with superlatives; prepositions after superlatives. Example sentences from the article (85 extracted, saved to final_runs/run_004/extracted_examples.txt): 'Josh is taller than his sister.'; 'Joe's older than Mike. (comparing one person with another)'; 'Sheila is the youngest girl in the family. (comparing one person with the whole group she belongs to)'; 'I'm more interested in music than sport.'; 'The most frightening film I've ever seen was Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho.'; 'What is the least expensive way of travelling in Japan?'

- Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change y to i (busier, happiest, easier, funniest); other two-syllable adjectives (cleverer, quieter, narrower, simpler)

**Usage rules covered (visible in screenshots):**

- Using much, a lot, far with comparatives ("much better", "a lot more crowded", "far less intelligent")
- Using than with object pronouns ("stronger than me")
- "-er and -er" / "more and more" constructions ("hotter and hotter")
- "The -er, the -er" constructions ("The colder it is, the hungrier I get")
- less/least for lower degree ("the least expensive way")
